paras: The torture of a Chinese man near Marysville, California, took place in late July 1888, when a group of Chinese men at a garden across the Yuba River held a countryman suspended by a rope for three days as an accused thief. After a white man intervened, the captors promised to hand him to the authorities, but he was not seen again, and officers opened an investigation. A California Associated Press dispatch called it "shockingly barbarous treatment," and a Honolulu paper later reprinted it as "Chinese Lynch Law."
The victim worked as a domestic on a ranch near the garden. The Chinese at the garden were said to have threatened to kill anybody caught stealing from them.

Sometime in the week before August 1, a white man found the victim in a shed at the garden, hanging from a rope passed under his shoulders. The man said he had been kept in that position for three days without food or water. When the white man interceded, the captors told him that the prisoner was a thief who had been caught trying to steal from the owner's garden.

The captors were told that they must bring him to town and deliver him to the authorities. They lowered him to the ground and promised to bring him in, but, as the dispatch put it, "nothing has since been seen of him."
Officers of the law were investigating at the time of the August 1 dispatch. The coverage does not show what became of the victim, and no report of an arrest or prosecution was found.

The Sacramento Daily Record-Union ran the copyrighted California Associated Press dispatch on August 2 under the headlines "Mongolian Brutes" and "Barbarous Treatment of a Chinaman by His Countrymen." On August 27 the Pacific Commercial Advertiser of Honolulu reprinted a fuller text of the dispatch as "Chinese Lynch Law," including the captors' theft accusation. Both papers presented the episode as cruelty among Chinese men, calling the victim a "Chinaman," and neither named him or his captors.

reader.title: Torture of a Chinese man near Marysville, California
bases: Captors took the law into their own hands, suspending an accused thief by a rope for three days and having threatened to kill anyone caught stealing; A2 heads it 'Chinese Lynch Law' (A1, A2).

The victim was punished without legal authority by a group of captors of unstated size for alleged theft, but no death was reported; after the captors lowered him and promised to deliver him to the authorities, 'nothing has since been seen of him' (A1, A2).
Both articles print the same August 1 Marysville dispatch, so they are one source, not independent reports (A1, A2).

record_check.dossier: Late July 1888 ('within the past week' before the August 1 dispatch)
Two papers; first report Sacramento Daily Record-Union, 1888-08-02; the Honolulu item is a later reprint
Chinese countrymen of the victim at the garden
Suspended by a rope under the shoulders (not hanged by the neck) for three days without food or water; a general threat to kill thieves
No attempt to kill is reported; a standing threat to kill thieves and the victim's later disappearance; fate unknown
Held captive privately by the accusers, never in legal custody
